doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Moving to Los Angeles and the studio scene
summary: At his mother's and brother's urging he moved to Los Angeles, tried TV and studio work, and was labeled a jazz player not suited to studios.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: So the 60s were maybe kind of a difficult decade for jazz, at least in New York.

Also, since my brother was out here, I guess my mother was encouraging me, well why don’t you go try it out there, maybe there’s an opportunity to get into pictures or be close to your brother, and it’ll help you a little bit. So I did get out there. And then I did some T.V. shows out here, playing the studios, I did a few things with some of the studios. In fact he got me one of the earliest things, I’ll tell you about the Frank Sinatra flute earlier. But I had a flute solo to do with Felix Slatkin or one of the early things with one of the studios. And I wasn’t that experienced with orchestras, and I was a soloist. So what happens is if you kind of don’t make the grade on a few of these things, they label you right away. He says, “Oh he’s a great jazz player but he’s not the studio guy.” So I had a few opportunities when I wasn’t ready, but then I did a few T.V. shows, “The Barbara McNair Show” or some other stuff, and so I remember Frank Strazzeri, we were talking about that once, something he said, he was not in the studios either. He said, “Well you didn’t have your heart in it.” Or some people like gear themselves up for that, they train you know, have classical training or this or that. And he’d joked, he said, “Bebop ruined my life.” It was a joke, but what I meant was you know I had a few chances of doing that. So my brother was in the studios for about twenty years. But a few tests, and I think Patrick Williams, someone hired me, I got a call playing lead alto, like the alto solo behind a movie like [scats]. And I had to borrow an alto because I wasn’t ready, I didn’t have my own. Anyhow if you miss a few trials they label you, that’s what I meant to say.
They say, “Oh he’s a great jazz player but he’s not really ready for this.” What I mean is you don’t get too many chances.
That’s what I meant. So I probably missed a few things.
Well maybe it was fortunate because you ended up devoting more time to the jazz.

Yeah, that’s always been my love is the jazz, always. I hear some people in the studios, you probably heard it already, saying, “Well tomorrow we’ve got M1 and M2 and M16,” you know the studio cues they call it. “Turn the page, M3” [scats]. Next cue. That’s their life — I mean not their life — their musical life is they don’t go out and play too much but they have this down where they’re technically able to play. Sometimes it’s maybe more involved but you know, so I did a little bit of that. And M 19, okay [scats]. Next. M 20. And how you make the money and so on and so on. But I’ve always had the most fun performing and playing and playing jazz.
